questions.title: The coupling spring that the period ignores
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: C.1 Simple harmonic motion (defining equation a = -omega^2 x, period of a mass-spring oscillator, energy in SHM) and C.2 Wave model (travelling waves, the wave equation v = f lambda, phase difference and the propagation delay)
questions.subtopic: C.1 Simple harmonic motion and C.2 Wave model
questions.challenge_mechanism: In the symmetric normal mode the two gliders keep a constant separation, so the coupling spring is never stretched and its stiffness cancels completely from the equation of motion; the period is fixed by the wall springs alone, so the quantity the student instinctively reaches for is not the quantity that sets the frequency of the wave that is launched into the tube.

questions.question: Two identical gliders, each of mass $m=0.020\ \mathrm{kg}$, rest on a frictionless horizontal air track. Each glider is held to a fixed post by a spring of stiffness $k=2.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, and the two gliders are joined to each other by a coupling spring of stiffness $k_{c}=3.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ (see the figure). The left glider carries a light piston that closes the near end of a long straight tube; the far end of the tube is lined with an absorber, so a travelling wave rather than a standing wave is set up, and when the glider moves along the track the piston drives a longitudinal compression wave along the tube. The speed of sound in the air in the tube is $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Friction, the mass of the springs and the mass of the piston are all negligible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The two gliders are displaced by equal amounts in the same direction and released from rest. Show that the coupling spring is neither stretched nor compressed at any instant, deduce that the period of this motion is $T_{s}=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, and calculate the value of $T_{s}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gliders are now displaced by equal amounts in opposite directions and released from rest. Determine the period $T_{a}$ of this motion, showing how the coupling spring now contributes, and calculate the ratio $T_{s}/T_{a}$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In the antisymmetric motion the piston drives the wave in the tube at the frequency $f=1/T_{a}$. Calculate the frequency, the wavelength of the wave in the tube, and the phase difference between two points on the tube axis that are $0.534\ \mathrm{m}$ apart. State which of the two points is ahead in phase.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that $T_{s}/T_{a}=\sqrt{1+2k_{c}/k}$, and hence determine the value of this ratio in the limits $k_{c}\to0$ and $k_{c}\to\infty$. Explain what each limit means physically for the motion of the two gliders.

questions.answer:
**(a)** In this motion the two gliders have equal displacements in the same direction at every instant, so $x_{1}=x_{2}$ and their separation never changes; the coupling spring therefore remains at its natural length and exerts no force on either glider. **(M1)** Each glider is then acted on only by its own wall spring, so Newton's second law for either glider gives

$$m\ddot{x}=-kx\quad\Rightarrow\quad\ddot{x}=-\frac{k}{m}x.$$ **(A1)**

Comparing with the defining equation of simple harmonic motion, $a=-\omega^{2}x$, shows that $\omega_{s}=\sqrt{k/m}$ and hence

$$T_{s}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.020}{2.0\times10^{4}}}=2\pi\sqrt{1.0\times10^{-6}}$$ **(A1)**

$$T_{s}=6.28\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}=6.28\ \mathrm{ms}.$$ **(A1)**

The coupling stiffness $k_{c}$ does not appear: in this mode the coupling spring is inert.

**(b)** In the antisymmetric motion $x_{1}=-x_{2}$, so the separation of the gliders changes by $2x_{1}$ and the coupling spring is stretched or compressed by twice the displacement of either glider. **(M1)** Its force on a glider is therefore $-k_{c}(2x_{1})$, and combining this with the wall spring gives

$$m\ddot{x}_{1}=-kx_{1}-2k_{c}x_{1}=-(k+2k_{c})x_{1},$$ **(A1)**

so $\omega_{a}=\sqrt{(k+2k_{c})/m}$ and

$$T_{a}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k+2k_{c}}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.020}{2.0\times10^{4}+2(3.0\times10^{4})}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.020}{8.0\times10^{4}}}=2\pi\sqrt{2.5\times10^{-7}}$$

$$T_{a}=3.14\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}=3.14\ \mathrm{ms}.$$ **(A1)**

The ratio of the two periods is

$$\frac{T_{s}}{T_{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{k+2k_{c}}{k}}=\sqrt{\frac{8.0\times10^{4}}{2.0\times10^{4}}}=2.00.$$ **(A1)**

The antisymmetric mode is therefore the faster of the two.

**(c)** The piston is driven by the glider that moves in the antisymmetric mode, so the frequency of the wave in the tube is fixed by $T_{a}$:

$$f=\frac{1}{T_{a}}=\frac{1}{3.1416\times10^{-3}}=318\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ **(M1)(A1)**

Using the wave equation $v=f\lambda$,

$$\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{340}{318.3}=1.07\ \mathrm{m}.$$ **(A1)**

The phase difference between two points separated by $\Delta x=0.534\ \mathrm{m}$ is

$$\Delta\varphi=\frac{2\pi\,\Delta x}{\lambda}=\frac{2\pi(0.534)}{1.068}=3.14\ \mathrm{rad}=\pi.$$ **(A1)**

The two points are in antiphase. The point nearer the piston is ahead in phase: the disturbance reaches it first, and the farther point lags by the propagation delay $\Delta x/v=1.57\ \mathrm{ms}$, which is exactly half a period.

**(d)** Dividing the two periods,

$$\frac{T_{s}}{T_{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{k+2k_{c}}{k}}=\sqrt{1+\frac{2k_{c}}{k}}.$$ **(M1)**

As $k_{c}\to0$ the ratio tends to $1$, so $T_{a}\to T_{s}$. The coupling spring has gone, the two gliders are independent identical oscillators, and every possible motion is a superposition of one single frequency; the distinction between the symmetric and the antisymmetric mode therefore disappears. **(A1)**

As $k_{c}\to\infty$ the ratio diverges and $T_{a}\to0$. An infinitely stiff coupling spring holds the gliders a fixed distance apart, so they can no longer move in opposite directions and the antisymmetric mode is suppressed. **(A1)**

For any finite $k_{c}$ the ratio is greater than one, so the antisymmetric mode is always the faster of the two, while the symmetric period is completely independent of $k_{c}$. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) requires the explicit statement that equal displacements in the same direction leave the coupling spring at its natural length. A candidate who writes $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/(k+k_{c})}$ or $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/(k+2k_{c})}$ has assumed that the coupling spring acts and forfeits the mark; this is the error the question is built to expose. The two (A1)s are for obtaining $\omega_{s}=\sqrt{k/m}$ by comparison with $a=-\omega^{2}x$, and for the numerical period. Accept $6.3\ \mathrm{ms}$, $2\pi\ \mathrm{ms}$ or $6.28\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$.

(b) The (M1) is for recognising that the coupling spring's extension is twice the individual displacement; a candidate who uses $k_{c}x_{1}$ instead of $2k_{c}x_{1}$ obtains $\omega_{a}=\sqrt{(k+k_{c})/m}=1.6\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and a ratio of $1.58$, which forfeits the last two marks but should still be followed through in (c) and (d). Accept the ratio as $2$, $2.0$ or $2.00$.

(c) Follow-through from (b) is expected: if the candidate's $T_{a}$ differs, the frequency, the wavelength and the phase difference must be recomputed consistently with it and are then credited. The phase-difference mark requires the substitution $\Delta\varphi=2\pi\Delta x/\lambda$, not a quoted $\pi$; accept $3.1\ \mathrm{rad}$, $180^{\circ}$ or $\pi$. The statement of which point leads carries no separate mark, but a candidate who says the farther point leads has reversed the propagation direction and should be corrected.

(d) The (M1) requires the ratio to be written as $\sqrt{1+2k_{c}/k}$; a candidate who states the two limits without deriving the ratio earns at most one mark. Both limits and both physical explanations are needed. Do not accept 'the ratio becomes zero' for $k_{c}\to0$; it becomes one.
questions.explanation:
The question is built on a single point of physics: in the symmetric normal mode of this system the coupling spring does not change length, so it cannot affect the period. A candidate who has met a coupled oscillator reaches for the coupling stiffness, and the natural guess is that the period must involve $k+k_{c}$ or $k+2k_{c}$. In the symmetric mode it involves neither; only the wall springs and the mass appear, and the period is exactly that of a single glider on its own wall spring.

The reason is that the two gliders move as one. Their separation is constant, the coupling spring stays at its natural length, and it pulls on neither glider. The wall springs are the only sources of restoring force, and each acts on its own glider, so the two oscillators are independent and identical. The coupling spring matters only in the antisymmetric mode, where the gliders move towards and away from each other: the separation changes by twice the displacement of one glider, so the spring's extension is doubled and its effective stiffness is $2k_{c}$. This is the familiar result that a spring pulled from both ends behaves as though it were twice as stiff.

Part (c) forces the SHM result to do work. The wave frequency is not chosen by the candidate; it is fixed by $T_{a}$, and the wavelength then follows from $v=f\lambda$. The phase difference is the wave-model consequence: two points half a wavelength apart are in antiphase, and the point nearer the source leads. A candidate who uses the naive $f=\sqrt{k/m}/(2\pi)$, the symmetric frequency, will obtain a wavelength twice too large and a phase difference half the correct value; the question separates those two frequencies deliberately.

Part (d) turns the result into a limit. Writing the ratio as $\sqrt{1+2k_{c}/k}$ makes both limits visible. As the coupling stiffness vanishes the two frequencies coalesce, which is the signature of a degeneracy: without coupling there is no way to tell the 'symmetric' mode from the 'antisymmetric' one, because the two gliders are simply independent. As the coupling stiffness becomes very large the gliders are locked a fixed distance apart and the antisymmetric motion is frozen out.

Classic wrong turns: assuming that the coupling spring contributes to the symmetric mode; treating the two gliders as a single mass $2m$ on a single spring, which happens to give the right answer here only because of the factor of two; and using the symmetric frequency rather than the antisymmetric one to drive the wave.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the C.1 bullets on the defining equation of SHM and the period of a mass-spring oscillator, combined with the C.2 bullets on travelling waves, the wave equation and phase difference. The design is original in its arc: the two normal modes of a symmetrically anchored pair of gliders are contrasted so that the coupling stiffness cancels in one of them, and that same system then drives a longitudinal wave whose frequency, wavelength and phase structure are read off from the SHM result. The values $m=0.020\ \mathrm{kg}$, $k=2.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ and $k_{c}=3.0\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ were chosen so that the two angular frequencies are exactly $1000$ and $2000\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, making the period ratio exactly $2$ and the wavelength $0.34\pi\ \mathrm{m}$, and so that the two probe points are separated by exactly half a wavelength.

verification.method: Both normal-mode frequencies were obtained from the equations of motion and re-checked by substituting the modal forms x1 = x2 and x1 = -x2; the antisymmetric effective stiffness k + 2k_c was verified; the wave frequency was taken as 1/T_a and the wavelength and phase difference recomputed from lambda = v/f and delta_phi = 2 pi delta_x / lambda; the propagation delay was checked to equal half of T_a.

questions.title: The touch that silences the first seven harmonics
questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: C.4 Standing waves and resonance (boundary conditions, nodes and antinodes, the harmonic series of a string fixed at both ends, resonance conditions)
questions.challenge_mechanism: Touching the string three-eighths of the way along does not split it into two independent strings but forces a single node there, and because the nodes of the nth mode fall at multiples of L/n the mode number must be a multiple of 8; the lowest note the touched string can give is therefore not the fundamental, and not the third harmonic that the familiar one-third touch would produce, but the eighth harmonic.

figure.caption: A string of length L = 0.80 m is fixed at both ends and drawn vibrating in its eighth harmonic, which has nine nodes including the two ends. A finger holds the string at a node a distance d = 0.30 m from the left support; the eighth harmonic is the lowest mode whose node pattern already contains that point.

questions.question: A string of length $L=0.80\ \mathrm{m}$ is stretched between two rigid supports with a tension $T=24\ \mathrm{N}$. Its linear mass density is $\mu=0.015\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}}$, and the tension may be taken as uniform along the whole string. A player lightly touches the string at a point a distance $d$ from the left support, holding that point fixed, and then sets the string vibrating; the touch forces a node at that point but does not otherwise alter the string. Only a standing wave that already has a node at the touched point can be excited.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of transverse waves on the string, and calculate the frequencies of the first three standing-wave modes of the string when it is not touched.

parts.label: b
parts.text: With the string touched at $d=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$, show that a standing wave can be excited only if the mode number $n$ satisfies $d=jL/n$ for some integer $j$, deduce that $n$ must be a multiple of $8$, and hence determine the lowest frequency that the touched string can produce.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the frequencies of the next two modes that the touched string can produce, and determine the total number of nodes, including the two fixed ends, in the lowest of these allowed modes. State how many of the untouched harmonics below that lowest allowed frequency are absent.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The player now touches the string at its midpoint instead. Explain how the set of allowed modes changes, determine the new lowest frequency, and explain why every odd harmonic is now missing.

questions.answer:
**(a)** For a stretched string the wave speed is given by $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$: **(M1)**

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{24}{0.015}}=\sqrt{1600}=40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$ **(A1)**

The standing-wave condition for a string fixed at both ends is $L=n\lambda/2$, so $f_{n}=nv/(2L)$: **(M1)**

$$f_{n}=\frac{n(40)}{2(0.80)}=25n\ \mathrm{Hz},$$

giving $f_{1}=25\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $f_{2}=50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{3}=75\ \mathrm{Hz}$. **(A1)**

**(b)** A standing wave on the string has zero displacement at every node, and the nodes of the $n$th mode lie at distances $x_{j}=jL/n$ from the left support, with $j=0,1,2,\dots,n$. **(M1)** The touched point is held fixed, so it must be a node, and therefore $d=jL/n$ for some integer $j$. **(A1)** Substituting $d=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ and $L=0.80\ \mathrm{m}$,

$$n=\frac{jL}{d}=\frac{j(0.80)}{0.30}=\frac{8j}{3}.$$ **(A1)**

For $n$ to be an integer, $j$ must be a multiple of $3$, so $j=3,6,9,\dots$ and the mode number must be $n=8,16,24,\dots$ — a multiple of $8$. **(A1)** The lowest allowed mode is therefore $n=8$, with frequency

$$f=\frac{8v}{2L}=\frac{8(40)}{1.60}=200\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ **(A1)**

**(c)** The next two allowed modes are $n=16$ and $n=24$: **(M1)**

$$f_{16}=16\times25=400\ \mathrm{Hz},\qquad f_{24}=24\times25=600\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ **(A1)**

In the $n=8$ mode the nodes lie at $x_{j}=j(0.80)/8=0.10j\ \mathrm{m}$ for $j=0,1,\dots,8$, that is at $0.00,0.10,0.20,\dots,0.80\ \mathrm{m}$. Counting the two fixed ends, there are $9$ nodes in all. **(A1)** The untouched harmonics below $200\ \mathrm{Hz}$ are $25,50,75,100,125,150$ and $175\ \mathrm{Hz}$ — seven of them — and all seven are absent. **(A1)**

**(d)** Touching at the midpoint sets $d=L/2$, so $n=jL/d=2j$ and only even mode numbers survive: the allowed frequencies are $50,100,150,\dots\ \mathrm{Hz}$. **(M1)** The new lowest frequency is therefore the second harmonic,

$$f=\frac{2v}{2L}=\frac{2(40)}{1.60}=50\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$ **(A1)**

Every odd harmonic has an antinode at the midpoint, so holding the midpoint fixed suppresses all of them; only the even harmonics, which already have a node there, are unaffected. **(A1)** In general a touch at a distance $L/p$ from one end selects the harmonics whose numbers are multiples of $p$: the midpoint touch ($p=2$) keeps the even harmonics, and the one-third touch ($p=3$) keeps every third.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The first (M1) is for $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$; a candidate who writes $v=T/\mu$ or $v=\sqrt{\mu/T}$ forfeits it. Accept $40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the set $25\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $75\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Follow-through applies: a wrong $v$ propagates consistently through (b) to (d) and those marks remain available.

(b) The essential step is that the touched point is held at zero displacement and is therefore a node. A candidate who instead treats the touch as cutting the string into two independent segments and looks for a frequency common to both will usually reach the same lowest answer here, but that is not the intended reasoning; award the method mark only if the node condition is stated. The (A1) for $n=8j/3$ must come from substituting $d=0.30$ and $L=0.80$. A candidate who assumes that a touch at three-eighths of the length gives the eighth harmonic by analogy with the familiar one-half and one-third cases earns nothing unless the condition is derived.

(c) Accept $400\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $600\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The node count must include the two fixed ends; a candidate who reports $8$ nodes has counted only the interior nodes and loses the mark. Accept the number seven or the explicit list $25$ to $175\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

(d) The (M1) is for $n=2j$, and the new lowest frequency is $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The final mark requires the reason to be stated in terms of the midpoint: odd harmonics have an antinode at the centre, while even harmonics already have a node there. 'Because the string is halved' is not sufficient, since the two halves are not independent in this situation.
questions.explanation:
A stretched string fixed at both ends is the standard example of a harmonic series, and the result $f_{n}=nv/(2L)$ is the first thing a candidate reaches for. The question is designed so that this formula is not the answer. Touching the string at a point does not divide it into two independent strings; it forces a node there, and the whole string must still vibrate as a single standing wave. The modes that can be excited are therefore exactly those whose own node pattern already contains the touched point.

For a mode with $n$ half-wavelengths along the string, the nodes lie at $jL/n$. Requiring one of them to coincide with the touch at $d$ gives $d=jL/n$, or $n=jL/d$. With $d=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ and $L=0.80\ \mathrm{m}$ this is $n=8j/3$, and because $n$ must be an integer the smallest possible mode number is $8$, not $1$ and not $3$. The lowest note the touched string can give is the eighth harmonic, at $200\ \mathrm{Hz}$ — eight times the fundamental.

The arithmetic is a number-theoretic condition rather than an algebraic one: the touch point is three-eighths of the way along, and $8/3$ only becomes an integer when it is multiplied by three. This is why the familiar cases are the easy ones. Touching at the midpoint gives $n=2j$ and the even harmonics; touching at one third of the length gives $n=3j$ and the third, sixth and ninth. The three-eighths position is deliberately not one of these, so a candidate who tries to generalise from the familiar cases without deriving the node condition will fail.

Part (c) also asks for the node count, which tests whether the candidate has understood that the touched point is a node and not a new end: the eighth mode has nine nodes, not eight, because the two fixed ends count.

The classic wrong turns are: quoting $f_{n}=nv/(2L)$ and reporting $25\ \mathrm{Hz}$ as the lowest available note; treating the touch as cutting the string into two separate strings of length $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ and $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ and searching for their common resonances, which can give the right number for the wrong reason; and forgetting that the fixed ends are nodes when counting. There is also a practical check worth making: on a real instrument the touched harmonic is much weaker than the open string, because the finger damps the other modes and forces the energy into the one pattern that has a node beneath it.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the C.4 bullets on boundary conditions, nodes and antinodes and the harmonic series of a string fixed at both ends. The design is original in its arc: rather than quoting the standard harmonic series, the candidate must derive the condition that the touched point be a node, and the touch point was chosen at three-eighths of the length so that the mode number must be a multiple of 8 rather than the obvious 2 or 3. The values $L=0.80\ \mathrm{m}$, $T=24\ \mathrm{N}$ and $\mu=0.015\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}}$ were chosen so that the wave speed is exactly $40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the untouched harmonics are the round numbers $25n\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and the lowest allowed mode is exactly the eighth harmonic at $200\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

verification.method: Wave speed from v = sqrt(T/mu) = 40 m/s; the harmonic series recomputed as f_n = n v/(2L) = 25n Hz; the node condition d = jL/n solved as n = jL/d = 8j/3, giving n = 8, 16, 24 and f = 200, 400, 600 Hz; the node spacing L/8 = 0.10 m and the nine-node count checked; the midpoint case solved as n = 2j giving a lowest frequency of 50 Hz.
